title: Stephen
lead: Stephen, a Greek-speaking Jewish believer chosen as one of the Seven in Jerusalem, was a preacher and miracle-worker whose speech before the Sanhedrin retold Israel's story and ended in his stoning. Christians honor him as the first martyr, and his death set off the persecution that carried the gospel out of Jerusalem.

sections.b: Acts introduces Stephen as "full of faith and the Holy Spirit," first among the Seven chosen to see to the daily serving of the widows (Acts 6:1–6). He quickly appears as a worker of wonders and a debater in the Greek-speaking synagogues of Jerusalem (Acts 6:8–10). Accused of speaking against the temple and the law, he answers with the longest speech in Acts (Acts 7:2–53), a retelling of Israel's history from Abraham to Solomon that turns into a charge of resisting the Holy Spirit. He sees the Son of Man standing at God's right hand, prays to Jesus to receive his spirit and to forgive his killers, and dies under stones while a young man named Saul looks on (Acts 7:54–8:1).

Luke makes Stephen the hinge of Acts. His death scatters the believers through Judea and Samaria (Acts 8:1–4; Acts 11:19), fulfilling the plan of Acts 1:8, and introduces Saul, the future Paul. His speech gathers themes that run through the New Testament: God meets his people outside the land and the temple, Israel rejected the deliverers God sent, and the Most High does not live in what hands have made (compare John 4:21–24; Hebrews 8–10). His death mirrors Jesus' own (Luke 23:34, 46).

The churches call Stephen the protomartyr, the first martyr, and the first deacon (Irenaeus already calls him so). His feast is kept on December 26 in the West and December 27 in the East. In AD 415 a priest named Lucian reported finding his tomb near Jerusalem, and relics of Stephen spread across the Mediterranean; Augustine records healings at a shrine of Stephen in North Africa (City of God 22.8). The empress Eudocia built a basilica in his honor north of Jerusalem's Damascus Gate in the 400s.
